finalAnswer: For each possible right-angle vertex, multiply its longest available horizontal leg by its longest available vertical leg. Output the largest product; it is twice the maximum area.
shortExplanation: Every allowed triangle has a right angle where its horizontal and vertical sides meet. At that corner, the two leg choices can be maximized independently.
detailedSteps: **Fix a corner.** For post $i$, scan all other posts. Let $H_i$ be the largest $|x_j-x_i|$ among posts with $y_j=y_i$, and let $V_i$ be the largest $|y_j-y_i|$ among posts with $x_j=x_i$. A missing leg gives length zero.

**Bound and attain the area.** An allowed triangle with corner $i$ has doubled area equal to its horizontal leg times its vertical leg, so it is at most $H_iV_i$. When both maxima are positive, choose a post attaining each. They are different posts: a single post sharing both coordinates with the corner would contradict distinctness and positive leg length. These choices therefore form a valid triangle attaining $H_iV_i$.

**Cover all valid triangles.** The horizontal and vertical sides of any triangle share a vertex, which must be one of the posts considered as a corner. Taking the maximum product over all corners cannot miss an allowed triangle. The source guarantees that at least one valid triangle exists, so at least one product is positive.

**Use the requested doubled area.** The product is already twice the area; do not divide it by two. Coordinate differences are at most $20000$, so the product is at most $400000000$. Integer arithmetic suffices, and the implementation uses 64-bit values throughout. The scan costs $O(N^2)$ time and $O(N)$ memory for the input points. It reads triangles.in and writes triangles.out.
keyIdeas: Choose the shared vertex of the perpendicular sides.
Independent longest-leg choices give a matching upper bound and construction.
commonMistakes: Printing area rather than twice the area.
Using a diagonal side as a leg or forgetting absolute differences.
Confusing this Bronze maximum-area task with the different same-name Silver task.
alternativeMethods: Enumerate all triples of distinct posts, check that a horizontal side and a vertical side are present, and evaluate the doubled area by a determinant. This $O(N^3)$ method also fits $N\le100$ and is a useful independent checker.
difficultyNotes: A short geometric optimization. The proof needs to justify that the two maximum leg choices form a real triangle.

finalAnswer: Output the number of maximal contiguous runs of positions where $A_i\ne B_i$.
shortExplanation: Flipping each mismatch run corrects it in one operation. An interval toggle can remove at most two mismatch boundaries, which proves that fewer operations cannot suffice.
detailedSteps: **Mark mismatches.** Let $d_i=1$ when the desired and actual breeds differ, and $d_i=0$ otherwise. Since there are exactly two breeds, toggling a substring toggles precisely those mismatch bits. Count positions whose bit is one and whose preceding bit is zero, treating the position before the string as zero.

**Construct a solution.** If there are $r$ maximal one-runs, flip each corresponding substring once. Every mismatch is toggled exactly once and no matching position changes, so this uses $r$ operations and produces the desired string.

**Prove the lower bound, including overlapping operations.** Pad the mismatch string with $d_0=d_{N+1}=0$ and define boundary bits $$e_i=d_i\oplus d_{i-1}\qquad(1\le i\le N+1).$$ Each one-run has two boundaries, so initially there are $2r$ one-valued boundary bits. A flip on positions $l,\ldots,u$ toggles only $e_l$ and $e_{u+1}$: interior boundaries have both neighboring mismatch bits toggled and do not change. One operation can therefore reduce the boundary count by at most two. Reaching the all-zero target requires at least $r$ operations, even if intervals overlap or temporarily disturb correct positions. The construction attains this bound.

**Count without editing the strings.** Keep a Boolean for whether the previous position was a mismatch. Increment the answer only at a new mismatch run. If the strings already agree, the result is zero; runs at either endpoint are counted normally. The program takes $O(N)$ time and $O(N)$ memory for the two strings, with $O(1)$ additional state. It reads breedflip.in and writes breedflip.out.
keyIdeas: Compare positions rather than rearranging cows.
Boundary parity gives a lower bound valid for arbitrary interval flips.
commonMistakes: Counting every mismatched position rather than every run.
Merging separated runs while forgetting that the matching gap would also toggle.
Reversing the order of a substring instead of toggling its breeds.
alternativeMethods: The answer is also half the number of changes between adjacent bits in the zero-padded mismatch string. Scanning the starts of one-runs avoids needing to divide a boundary count.
difficultyNotes: The implementation is introductory. The boundary argument explains why overlapping flips cannot improve the run-by-run construction.

finalAnswer: Build the old-position map $p$ for one ordered pair of reversals. At zero-based final position $i$, output $p^K(i)+1$, computing the power by repeated squaring.
shortExplanation: Both reversals together form one fixed permutation. Its binary powers replace up to a billion literal repetitions.
detailedSteps: **Build the combined map in the correct order.** Begin with indices $0,\ldots,N-1$, reverse the source interval $A$ first, then interval $B$. The resulting value $p(i)$ tells which old position supplies the label at new position $i$. This is a source-position map, rather than a cow’s destination map. One-based inclusive interval $[l,u]$ becomes the C++ half-open range from begin()+l-1 to begin()+u.

**Justify repeated composition.** For any old line $L$, one complete process gives $$L^\prime_i=L_{p(i)}.$$ A second process gives $L_{p(p(i))}$, and induction gives $L_{p^K(i)}$ after $K$ repetitions. The initial label at index $j$ is $j+1$, so the required label is $p^K(i)+1$. Reversal bijections and their compositions keep every index in range.

**Use binary powers.** Maintain an identity result map and a current power map. At bit $j$, the power is $p^{2^j}$. If that bit of $K$ is set, compose it into the result by answer[i]=power[answer[i]]. Both maps are powers of the same permutation, so the exponents add. Then square with next[i]=power[power[i]], using a separate vector so partial updates cannot corrupt composition. Divide the remaining exponent by two and continue. The invariant proves that the final result is exactly $p^K$.

**Respect the original bounds and output.** The source gives strict endpoints $l<u$ for both intervals; together they require at least two positions even though the separate bound on $N$ starts at one. There are at most 30 exponent bits for $K\le10^9$, giving $O(N\log K)$ time and $O(N)$ memory. Convert indices to labels only at the end, then print one label per line. Read swap.in and write swap.out. This is the two-reversal Bronze task, not the different Silver task.
keyIdeas: Combine ordered operations into one permutation before exponentiating.
Distinguish a source-position map from a destination map.
Use a separate vector when squaring a map.
commonMistakes: Applying the intervals in the opposite order.
Taking powers of the two reversals separately rather than of their combined process.
Printing zero-based indices or printing all labels on one line.
alternativeMethods: Decompose the combined permutation into cycles. For each position, move forward by $K$ modulo its cycle length. This gives $O(N)$ time after constructing the map and provides another way to avoid literal repetition. Keep the same source-position convention when converting the cycles into output labels.
difficultyNotes: A compact permutation-power implementation. Direction, interval endpoints and the order of composition matter more than the exponent size.
